strings.cat.title: Catechism
strings.cat.subtitle: The essentials of the faith
strings.cat.intro: A pocket catechism: what the Church believes, how she worships, how we are called to live, and how we pray. Grouped by the four pillars of the Catechism of the Catholic Church.
strings.cat.creed.title: What We Believe
strings.cat.creed.summary: The Creed — the heart of the faith professed by Christians since the age of the Apostles.
strings.cat.sacraments.title: The Seven Sacraments
strings.cat.sacraments.summary: Efficacious signs of grace, instituted by Christ and entrusted to the Church.
strings.cat.confession.title: How to Make a Confession
strings.cat.confession.summary: A simple step-by-step guide to the Sacrament of Penance and Reconciliation.
strings.cat.commandments.title: The Ten Commandments
strings.cat.commandments.summary: The law God gave through Moses, summed up in love of God and neighbour.
strings.cat.gifts.title: Gifts of the Holy Spirit
strings.cat.gifts.summary: Seven gifts that perfect the soul and dispose us to follow the Holy Spirit.
strings.cat.fruits.title: Fruits of the Holy Spirit
strings.cat.fruits.summary: Twelve perfections the Spirit forms in us as a foretaste of eternal glory.
strings.cat.virtues.title: The Virtues
strings.cat.virtues.summary: The three theological and four cardinal virtues that shape a good life.
strings.cat.sins.title: The Seven Capital Sins
strings.cat.sins.summary: The root vices — and the virtues that overcome each of them.
strings.cat.beatitudes.title: The Beatitudes
strings.cat.beatitudes.summary: The blueprint of Christian happiness from the Sermon on the Mount.
strings.cat.mercy.title: The Works of Mercy
strings.cat.mercy.summary: Seven corporal and seven spiritual works — love of neighbour in action.
strings.cat.precepts.title: Precepts, Holy Days & Fasting
strings.cat.precepts.summary: The minimum duties of a practising Catholic and the Church's days of observance.
strings.art.trinity.title: The Holy Trinity
strings.art.trinity.lead: One God in three divine Persons.
strings.art.trinity.p1: The central mystery of the Christian faith is the Holy Trinity: there is one God, who is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The three Persons are distinct, yet each is fully and equally the one God, sharing one divine nature.
strings.art.trinity.li1: The Father — creator and source of all life.
strings.art.trinity.li2: The Son — Jesus Christ, the Word made flesh, our Redeemer.
strings.art.trinity.li3: The Holy Spirit — the Lord and giver of life, who sanctifies us.
strings.art.trinity.callout.title: We profess it at every prayer
strings.art.trinity.callout.body: Every Sign of the Cross and Glory Be confesses the Trinity: in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.
strings.art.trinity.quote: Go, therefore, and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.
strings.art.creeds.title: The Creeds
strings.art.creeds.lead: The Church's summary of the faith in a few lines.
strings.art.creeds.p1: A creed is a concise statement of belief. The Church treasures two above all: the ancient Apostles' Creed, the baptismal symbol of the Church of Rome, and the fuller Nicene Creed, professed at Mass on Sundays and solemnities.
strings.art.creeds.li1: The Apostles' Creed — the oldest Roman baptismal profession.
strings.art.creeds.li2: The Nicene Creed — drawn from the Councils of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381).
strings.art.creeds.cards.title: Pray the Creeds
strings.art.creeds.apostles.description: The ancient baptismal profession of the Church of Rome.
strings.art.creeds.nicene.description: The creed of Nicaea and Constantinople, professed at Mass.
strings.art.creeds.history.title: One faith, clearly professed.
strings.art.creeds.history.body: From the earliest Church to today, the Creeds unite believers in the same faith, expressed clearly and faithfully.
strings.cat.scripture.title: Sacred Scripture
strings.cat.scripture.summary: Where the Bible came from, and why we can trust it.
strings.art.bible.title: Who Created the Bible?
strings.art.bible.lead: God inspired it. People wrote it. The Church gave it to us.
strings.art.bible.p0: The Bible did not write itself. God inspired it, human authors wrote it, and the Church gave us the Bible we have today. God + human authors + the Holy Spirit = The Holy Bible.
strings.art.bible.p1.title: God is the Ultimate Author
strings.art.bible.p1.body: God is the source of all truth. He inspired the human authors so that what they wrote is truly his Word: “All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching.”
strings.art.bible.p2.title: Human Authors Wrote the Bible
strings.art.bible.p2.body: About forty different human authors, from every walk of life — kings, priests, farmers, fishermen, a doctor, shepherds, a tax collector — writing in different places and times. They used their own words and writing styles, but were guided by the Holy Spirit.
strings.art.bible.p3.title: Written Over a Long Period
strings.art.bible.p3.body: The Bible was written over some 1,600 years, from Moses (about 1400 BC) to St John (about 100 AD). It is not one book but a library, gathered across the centuries.
strings.art.bible.p4.title: Inspired by the Holy Spirit
strings.art.bible.p4.body: The Holy Spirit guided the authors so that they wrote what God wants us to know. Inspiration does not mean God dictated every word, but that he ensured the truth without error in the original writings.
strings.art.bible.p5.title: The Church Discerned the Canon
strings.art.bible.p5.body: The early Church recognised which books were truly inspired. Through councils and the guidance of the Holy Spirit, the Church gave us the official list of 73 books — the Councils of Rome (382), Hippo (393) and Carthage (397 and 419). These councils did not create the Bible; they recognised the books already used in the Church.
strings.art.bible.p6.title: Handed Down by the Church
strings.art.bible.p6.body: The Church preserved, copied, and taught the Scriptures through every age. Without the Church we would not have the Bible today: the Church preserved it, protected it, and gave it to the world.
strings.cat.step.bible_journey.title: The Journey of the Bible
strings.cat.step.bible_journey.intro: From God's revelation to the book in your hands.
strings.step.bible.reveals.title: God Reveals His Word
strings.step.bible.reveals.body: God reveals himself and his plan for our salvation.
strings.step.bible.write.title: Human Authors Write
strings.step.bible.write.body: About forty authors write under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.
strings.step.bible.discern.title: The Church Discerns
strings.step.bible.discern.body: The early Church discerns which books are truly inspired.
strings.step.bible.preserve.title: The Church Preserves
strings.step.bible.preserve.body: The Church copies, preaches, and preserves the Scriptures.
strings.step.bible.reaches.title: The Bible Reaches Us
strings.step.bible.reaches.body: We receive the Bible through the Church, to know and love God.
strings.art.bible.remember.title: Remember
strings.art.bible.remember4: The Church gave us the Bible.
strings.art.bible.bottom.title: The bottom line
strings.art.bible.bottom.body: The Bible is not a book that came from nowhere. It has a divine Author, human writers, the Holy Spirit's guidance, and the Church's recognition and preservation. That is why the Bible is the Word of God, trusted by the Church.
strings.art.bible.quote: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.”
strings.art.marks.title: The Four Marks of the Church
strings.art.marks.p1: In the Nicene–Constantinopolitan Creed we profess that the Church is One, Holy, Catholic, and Apostolic. She is one body in Christ, built on him as the cornerstone and on the foundation of the Apostles.
strings.art.marks.li1: One — The Church is one because we have one Lord, one faith, one Baptism.
strings.art.marks.li2: Holy — Christ is her source of holiness, and she is called to lead people to holiness.
strings.art.marks.li3: Catholic — “Catholic” means universal: for all peoples, in all places, in all times.
strings.art.marks.li4: Apostolic — Founded on the Apostles, preserving their teaching through Apostolic Succession.
strings.art.marks.why.title: Why these marks matter
strings.art.marks.why.body: These four marks are not just titles. They are gifts from Christ that show who his Church is and what her mission is in the world.
strings.art.marks.closing.title: This is our Church
strings.art.marks.closing.body: The Church is not perfect because of us, but because of Christ who founded her. One, Holy, Catholic, and Apostolic — this is our faith, and this is the Church founded by Christ.
strings.art.last.title: The Last Things
strings.art.last.lead: One life. One choice. Eternal consequences.
strings.art.sacrament.title: What Is a Sacrament?
strings.art.sacrament.lead: An outward sign, instituted by Christ, to give grace.
strings.art.sacrament.p1: The seven sacraments are efficacious signs of grace, instituted by Christ and entrusted to the Church, by which divine life is given to us. They touch every stage and important moment of Christian life.
strings.art.sacrament.li1: Sacraments of Initiation — Baptism, Confirmation, and the Eucharist.
strings.art.sacrament.li2: Sacraments of Healing — Penance and the Anointing of the Sick.
strings.art.sacrament.li3: Sacraments at the Service of Communion — Holy Orders and Matrimony.
strings.art.confprayers.title: Prayers for Confession
strings.art.confprayers.lead: What to pray before, during, and after.
strings.art.confprayers.p1: A short examination of conscience prepares the heart; an act of contrition expresses our sorrow; a prayer of thanksgiving follows the grace of absolution.
strings.art.confprayers.cards.title: Related prayers
strings.art.great.title: The Two Great Commandments
strings.art.great.lead: On these two hang all the Law and the Prophets.
strings.art.great.quote: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart… and your neighbour as yourself.
strings.art.great.p1: Jesus summed up the whole Law in love: love of God and love of neighbour. The first three commandments concern our love of God; the remaining seven, our love of neighbour.
strings.art.giftsprayers.title: Praying to the Holy Spirit
strings.art.giftsprayers.p1: The gifts of the Holy Spirit, received in Baptism and strengthened in Confirmation, are stirred up by prayer. These ancient hymns and prayers call down the Spirit.
strings.art.giftsprayers.cards.title: Related prayers
strings.cat.fs.sacraments.title: The Seven Sacraments
strings.sac.baptism.label: Baptism
strings.sac.baptism.value: Frees from sin and makes us children of God and members of the Church.
strings.sac.confirmation.label: Confirmation
strings.sac.confirmation.value: Seals us with the Holy Spirit and strengthens us as witnesses of Christ.
strings.sac.eucharist.label: The Eucharist
strings.sac.eucharist.value: The true Body and Blood of Christ — source and summit of Christian life.
strings.sac.penance.label: Penance
strings.sac.penance.value: Reconciles us with God and the Church through absolution of sins.
strings.sac.anointing.label: Anointing of the Sick
strings.sac.anointing.value: Grace and comfort for the seriously ill and the dying.
strings.sac.orders.label: Holy Orders
strings.sac.orders.value: Consecrates bishops, priests, and deacons for sacred ministry.
strings.sac.matrimony.label: Matrimony
strings.sac.matrimony.value: Unites a man and woman in a lifelong covenant, an image of Christ's love.
strings.sac.group.service: Sacraments at the Service of Communion

strings.cmd.1.label: First
strings.cmd.1.value: I am the Lord your God; you shall have no strange gods before me.
strings.cmd.2.label: Second
strings.cmd.2.value: You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain.
strings.cmd.3.label: Third
strings.cmd.3.value: Remember to keep holy the Lord's Day.
strings.cmd.4.label: Fourth
strings.cmd.4.value: Honour your father and your mother.
strings.cmd.5.label: Fifth
strings.cmd.6.label: Sixth
strings.cmd.7.label: Seventh
strings.cmd.8.label: Eighth
strings.cmd.8.value: You shall not bear false witness against your neighbour.
strings.cmd.9.label: Ninth
strings.cmd.9.value: You shall not covet your neighbour's wife.
strings.cmd.10.label: Tenth
strings.cmd.10.value: You shall not covet your neighbour's goods.
strings.cat.fs.gifts.title: The Seven Gifts
strings.gift.wisdom.label: Wisdom
strings.gift.wisdom.value: To relish the things of God and see by his light.
strings.gift.understanding.label: Understanding
strings.gift.understanding.value: To grasp the truths of faith more deeply.
strings.gift.counsel.label: Counsel
strings.gift.counsel.value: Right judgement in choosing what is good.
strings.gift.fortitude.label: Fortitude
strings.gift.fortitude.value: Courage to do what is right, even in hardship.
strings.gift.knowledge.label: Knowledge
strings.gift.knowledge.value: To see created things rightly, in relation to God.
strings.gift.piety.label: Piety
strings.gift.piety.value: Loving devotion to God as a trusting child.
strings.gift.fear.label: Fear of the Lord
strings.gift.fear.value: Loving reverence and awe before God's majesty.
strings.cat.fs.fruits.title: The Twelve Fruits
strings.fruit.charity.label: Charity
strings.fruit.charity.value: Selfless love of God and neighbour.
strings.fruit.joy.label: Joy
strings.fruit.joy.value: Gladness rooted in God, not in circumstances.
strings.fruit.peace.label: Peace
strings.fruit.peace.value: Tranquillity of a soul resting in God.
strings.fruit.patience.label: Patience
strings.fruit.kindness.label: Kindness
strings.fruit.goodness.label: Goodness
strings.fruit.goodness.value: Uprightness that seeks the good of others.
strings.fruit.generosity.label: Generosity
strings.fruit.generosity.value: Open-handed giving of self and goods.
strings.fruit.gentleness.label: Gentleness
strings.fruit.faithfulness.label: Faithfulness
strings.fruit.modesty.label: Modesty
strings.fruit.self_control.label: Self-control
strings.fruit.chastity.label: Chastity
strings.fruit.chastity.value: Integrity of love according to one's state.
strings.cat.fs.virtues.title: The Seven Virtues
strings.virt.faith.label: Faith
strings.virt.faith.value: Believing in God and all he has revealed.
strings.virt.hope.label: Hope
strings.virt.hope.value: Trusting in God's promise of eternal life.
strings.virt.charity.label: Charity
strings.virt.charity.value: Loving God above all, and neighbour for his sake.
strings.virt.prudence.label: Prudence
strings.virt.prudence.value: Choosing the right means to the true good.
strings.virt.justice.label: Justice
strings.virt.justice.value: Giving God and neighbour their due.
strings.virt.fortitude.label: Fortitude
strings.virt.fortitude.value: Firmness and constancy in pursuing the good.
strings.virt.temperance.label: Temperance

strings.cat.fs.precepts.title: Duties & Days of Observance
strings.prec.1.label: First Precept
strings.prec.1.value: Attend Mass on Sundays and holy days, resting from servile work.
strings.prec.2.label: Second Precept
strings.prec.2.value: Confess your sins at least once a year.
strings.prec.3.label: Third Precept
strings.prec.3.value: Receive Holy Communion at least during the Easter season.
strings.prec.4.label: Fourth Precept
strings.prec.4.value: Keep holy the days of fasting and abstinence.
strings.prec.5.label: Fifth Precept
strings.prec.5.value: Provide for the material needs of the Church.
strings.prec.holydays.label: Holy Days of Obligation
strings.prec.holydays.value: Feasts on which the faithful attend Mass, as Sundays.
strings.prec.fasting.label: Fasting
strings.prec.fasting.value: One full meal on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday (ages 18–59).
strings.prec.abstinence.label: Abstinence
strings.prec.abstinence.value: No meat on Ash Wednesday and the Fridays of Lent (age 14+).
strings.prec.communion_fast.label: Eucharistic Fast
strings.prec.communion_fast.value: One hour without food or drink (except water) before Communion.
strings.cat.step.confession.title: How to Make a Good Confession
strings.cat.step.confession.intro: The Sacrament of Penance restores the grace of Baptism. If it has been a while, simply tell the priest — he will help you.
strings.conf.1.title: Examine your conscience
strings.conf.1.body: Prayerfully call to mind the sins committed since your last confession.
strings.conf.2.title: Be truly sorry
strings.conf.2.body: Make an act of contrition — sorrow for having offended God, whom we love.
strings.conf.3.title: Resolve to sin no more
strings.conf.3.body: Form a firm purpose of amendment to avoid sin and its occasions.
strings.conf.4.title: Begin the confession
strings.conf.4.body: Make the Sign of the Cross and say: 'Bless me, Father, for I have sinned. It has been [time] since my last confession.'
strings.conf.5.title: Confess your sins
strings.conf.5.body: Tell your sins simply and honestly, including the kind and number of grave sins.
strings.conf.6.title: Penance & Act of Contrition
strings.conf.6.body: Listen to the priest's counsel, accept your penance, and pray an Act of Contrition.
strings.conf.7.title: Receive absolution
strings.conf.7.body: The priest absolves you in the name of Christ. Give thanks to God and carry out your penance.
strings.art.last.intro: The Church has always taught four last things: death, judgement, heaven and hell. Behind them stands one simple truth — this life is the time of choosing, and what we choose here has consequences that do not end.
strings.art.last.earth.title: Earth — our earthly life
strings.art.last.earth.body: A time of trial and choice. Here we live, believe, love, repent, and choose whether to follow God. Death ends this earthly life: we do not return to another one.
strings.art.last.earth.ref: “It is appointed for mortals to die once, and after this comes judgement.” — Hebrews 9:27
strings.art.last.purgatory.title: Purgatory — final purification
strings.art.last.purgatory.body: For those who die in God's grace but are not yet perfectly purified. They are already assured of eternal salvation. Purgatory is not a second chance at salvation but a final purification, making the soul ready for heaven. The souls there are helped by the prayers of the faithful.
strings.art.last.heaven.title: Heaven — eternal communion with God
strings.art.last.heaven.body: The state of supreme and definitive happiness. Those who die in God's grace and are perfectly purified live for ever with Christ, and see God face to face.
strings.art.last.heaven.ref: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” — Matthew 5:8 · CCC 1023–1029
strings.art.last.hell.title: Hell — eternal separation from God
strings.art.last.hell.body: The state of definitive self-exclusion from communion with God. Those who die in mortal sin without repenting are separated from him for ever. God predestines no one to hell: it is the consequence of a free and deliberate turning away, persisted in to the end.
strings.art.last.sequence.title: The Catholic sequence
strings.art.last.seq.1: Earth — our earthly life, the time of choosing.
strings.art.last.seq.2: Death — the end of earthly life.
strings.art.last.seq.3: The Particular Judgement — each soul meets God's justice individually.
strings.art.last.seq.4: Heaven — for those who are already perfectly purified.
strings.art.last.seq.5: Purgatory, and then heaven — where purification is still needed.
strings.art.last.seq.6: Hell — for those who die in mortal sin without repentance.
strings.art.last.end.title: At the end of time
strings.art.last.end.body: At the end of time come the resurrection of the body and the Last Judgement, and then the fullness of God's kingdom — the new heavens and the new earth.
strings.art.last.remember.title: Remember
strings.art.last.remember.body: Earth is where we choose. Purgatory is where the saved are purified. Heaven is eternal life with God. Hell is eternal separation from God.
strings.art.angels.title: The Nine Choirs of Angels
strings.art.angels.lead: Praise, govern, serve — different choirs, one mission.
strings.art.angels.intro: Angels are purely spiritual creatures, with intelligence and will, who behold God and serve his plan. Christian tradition arranges them in nine choirs, grouped in three hierarchies. That arrangement is a theological framework rather than a defined doctrine — but it has shaped the Catholic imagination for fifteen centuries.
strings.art.angels.group.second: Second hierarchy — the governance of creation
strings.art.angels.group.third: Third hierarchy — ministers of God's providence
strings.art.angels.seraphim.title: Seraphim
strings.art.angels.seraphim.body: The burning ones, associated with the worship and contemplation of God. Isaiah saw them above the throne, each with six wings, calling to one another: “Holy, holy, holy.”
strings.art.angels.cherubim.title: Cherubim
strings.art.angels.cherubim.body: Associated with the fullness of divine knowledge and the contemplation of God's glory. They guard the way to the tree of life and bear up the throne of God.
strings.art.angels.thrones.title: Thrones
strings.art.angels.thrones.body: Traditionally associated with God's majesty and his judgement — the seat of his justice.
strings.art.angels.dominions.title: Dominions
strings.art.angels.dominions.body: Associated with authority, and with the ordering of the lower angelic choirs according to God's will.
strings.art.angels.virtues.title: Virtues
strings.art.angels.virtues.body: Traditionally associated with divine strength and the working of God's power in the world.
strings.art.angels.powers.title: Powers
strings.art.angels.powers.body: Associated with authority over spiritual forces, and with protection against the powers of evil.
strings.art.angels.principalities.title: Principalities
strings.art.angels.principalities.body: Associated with the governance of peoples, nations and communities.
strings.art.angels.archangels.title: Archangels
strings.art.angels.archangels.body: Angels entrusted with messages or missions of particular importance. Scripture names three: Michael, Gabriel and Raphael.
strings.art.angels.angels.title: Angels
strings.art.angels.angels.body: The lowest choir in the traditional ranking, and the nearest to us: fully spiritual beings who serve God and minister to humanity.
strings.art.angels.scripture.title: What Scripture names
strings.art.angels.scripture.body: The Bible names several kinds of angelic being — thrones, dominions, principalities and powers among them — but nowhere sets out a complete list of nine choirs. The names are scriptural; the ninefold ranking is not.
strings.art.angels.tradition.title: Where the order comes from
strings.art.angels.tradition.body: The ninefold arrangement is drawn from Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite and taken up by St Thomas Aquinas, who taught that the angels are diverse in their offices but united in their adoration of the one God.
strings.art.angels.clarify.title: What the Church actually teaches
strings.art.angels.clarify.body: The Church teaches that angels exist as spiritual, non-corporeal creatures, and that they serve God as his messengers (CCC 328–336). The nine choirs are a traditional theological classification, not a defined dogma: no Catholic is required to hold that Scripture lists exactly nine.
strings.art.angels.quote: “Bless the Lord, O you his angels, you mighty ones who do his word, obeying the voice of his word.”
strings.art.reverence.title: Types of Reverence
strings.art.reverence.intro: Catholics do not worship Mary, the saints or the angels. Worship — adoration — belongs to God alone. What is given to the saints is veneration: honour paid to God's grace at work in them. Theology has names for these different degrees of reverence, and the distinction between them matters.
strings.art.reverence.latria.title: Latria — worship
strings.art.reverence.latria.body: Worship and adoration, given to God alone. It is owed to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and to Christ present in the Blessed Sacrament. To give latria to any creature, however holy, would be idolatry.
strings.art.reverence.hyperdulia.title: Hyperdulia — the highest veneration
strings.art.reverence.hyperdulia.body: The highest veneration, given to the Blessed Virgin Mary because she is the Mother of God. It surpasses the honour given to any other creature — yet it remains veneration, and never becomes worship.
strings.art.reverence.protodulia.title: Protodulia — the foremost veneration
strings.art.reverence.protodulia.body: A term used for the first or foremost veneration among the saints, given to St Joseph as head of the Holy Family and patron of the universal Church.
strings.art.reverence.dulia.title: Dulia — veneration
strings.art.reverence.dulia.body: The veneration given to the saints and the angels on account of God's grace at work in them. In honouring them we honour the God who made them holy, and we ask their prayers as we would ask a friend's.
strings.art.reverence.short.title: In short
strings.art.reverence.short.2: Mary is given the highest veneration — hyperdulia.
strings.art.reverence.short.3: St Joseph is given the foremost veneration among the saints — protodulia.
strings.art.reverence.short.4: The saints and angels are venerated — dulia.
strings.art.reverence.notworship.title: Veneration is not worship
strings.art.reverence.notworship.body: The difference is one of kind, not merely of degree. However great the honour paid to Our Lady or to the saints, it is never the adoration owed to God — and no amount of veneration adds up to worship. The Second Council of Nicaea and the Council of Trent both taught this explicitly.
strings.art.reverence.proto.title: A word about protodulia
strings.art.reverence.proto.body: The classical distinction is threefold: latria, dulia and hyperdulia. Protodulia is a later term, used by theologians to express St Joseph's pre-eminence among the saints. It names a rank within dulia rather than a fourth kind of reverence.
strings.art.relics.title: Types of Relics
strings.art.relics.lead: The three classes of relics, and why the Church honours them.
strings.art.relics.intro: Relics are the physical remains of the saints, or objects closely connected with them. Christians have honoured them from the earliest centuries: around the year 155 the faithful of Smyrna gathered up the bones of the martyr Polycarp as more precious than jewels, and to this day a saint's relic is traditionally placed in the altar of a consecrated church. The Catechism counts the veneration of relics among the forms of piety that surround the Church's sacramental life (CCC 1674–1675). By custom, relics are sorted into three classes.
strings.art.relics.first.title: First-class relics
strings.art.relics.first.body: Parts of the saint's own body — bone, hair, blood, or the ashes of the body. These are relics in the fullest sense, and the most precious. A fragment of bone set in a reliquary, a lock of hair or a phial of blood are all first-class relics.
strings.art.relics.second.title: Second-class relics
strings.art.relics.second.body: Things the saint owned or used in life — clothing, a book, a rosary, a crucifix, a ring or a walking stick. They are not part of the body, but they were part of the saint's daily life and bear witness to it.
strings.art.relics.third.title: Third-class relics
strings.art.relics.third.body: Objects that have been touched to a first- or second-class relic — most often a small square of cloth, a holy card or a medal. They are honoured because of that contact, not because any holiness has passed into them, and shrines usually give them away freely.
strings.art.relics.third.what: Objects touched to a first- or second-class relic
strings.art.relics.scripture.title: Relics in Scripture
strings.art.relics.scripture.1: A dead man is thrown into the grave of Elisha and, touching the prophet's bones, comes back to life (2 Kings 13:21).
strings.art.relics.scripture.2: A woman who has suffered for twelve years touches the fringe of Jesus' cloak and is healed (Mark 5:25–29).
strings.art.relics.scripture.3: Handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched St Paul are carried to the sick, and they are cured (Acts 19:11–12).
strings.art.relics.notworship.title: Honoured, never worshipped
strings.art.relics.notworship.body: A relic has no power of its own. Venerating it is dulia — the honour given to the saints — and never the adoration owed to God alone. What is honoured is God's grace at work in the saint, whose body was a living member of Christ and a temple of the Holy Spirit, as the Council of Trent taught. Any favour obtained is God's gift, not the object's.
strings.art.relics.classes.title: About the three classes
strings.art.relics.classes.body: First, second and third class are a customary way of speaking, not a formal category of Church law. The Church's own norms distinguish instead between significant relics — the body of a saint or a notable part of it — and non-significant ones, such as small fragments or objects the saint used.
strings.art.relics.sale.title: Never for sale
strings.art.relics.sale.body: Canon law absolutely forbids the sale of sacred relics (CIC can. 1190 §1). Relics may be given, but never bought or sold.
strings.art.relics.quote: “We do not worship, we do not adore, for fear that we should bow down to the creature rather than to the Creator, but we venerate the relics of the martyrs in order the better to adore Him whose martyrs they are.”
strings.art.pillars.title: The Three Pillars of the Faith
strings.art.pillars.intro: God has revealed himself, and that revelation reaches us in two ways: Sacred Scripture, the Word of God set down in writing, and Sacred Tradition, the same Gospel handed on in the living Church. Both were entrusted to the Apostles and, through them, to the Church, whose teaching office — the Magisterium — guards and interprets them. Take away any one of the three and the other two lose their footing.
strings.art.pillars.scripture.title: Sacred Scripture — the written Word
strings.art.pillars.scripture.body: The Bible is the inspired Word of God, written by human authors under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, who wrote as true authors while God remained the true author of what they wrote. Its seventy-three books, in the Old and New Testaments, set out God's plan of salvation and give the Church the foundation of her faith and her moral teaching.
strings.art.pillars.tradition.title: Sacred Tradition — the living transmission
strings.art.pillars.tradition.body: Tradition is the same Gospel handed on, not a second body of doctrine beside the Bible. Christ preached before anything was written, and what the Apostles received they passed on by word as well as in writing. It lives in the Church's worship and sacraments, her creeds and prayers, and the witness of the saints — and it was Tradition that recognised which books belong in Scripture at all.
strings.art.pillars.magisterium.title: The Magisterium — the teaching office
strings.art.pillars.magisterium.body: The Magisterium is the living teaching office of the Church: the pope and the bishops in communion with him, the successors of Peter and the Apostles. Its task is to interpret the Word of God authentically, to keep the Church united in the truth, and to hand on what it has received — not to add to it.
strings.art.pillars.together.title: How they hold together
strings.art.pillars.together.1: Scripture is the Word of God committed to writing.
strings.art.pillars.together.2: Tradition hands that same Word on whole and living in the Church.
strings.art.pillars.together.3: The Magisterium interprets both with the authority Christ gave the Apostles.
strings.art.pillars.together.4: All three are moved by the Holy Spirit, who leads the Church into all truth.
strings.art.pillars.notthree.title: Not three separate sources
strings.art.pillars.notthree.body: Scripture and Tradition are not two rival deposits: they flow from the same divine wellspring and form one deposit of the Word of God. And the Magisterium is not a third source standing over them. The Second Vatican Council put it plainly: the teaching office is not above the Word of God but serves it, teaching only what has been handed on.
strings.art.pillars.smallt.title: Tradition and traditions
strings.art.pillars.smallt.body: Sacred Tradition, which comes from the Apostles, is not the same as the customs that grow up around it in different times and places. Those lesser traditions — devotions, disciplines, ways of doing things — can be kept, changed or set aside by the Church. Apostolic Tradition cannot.
strings.art.pillars.quote: “Sacred Tradition, Sacred Scripture and the Magisterium of the Church are so connected and associated that one of them cannot stand without the others.”
strings.art.images.title: Idols and Sacred Images
strings.art.images.lead: Why a crucifix is not an idol.
strings.art.images.intro: Catholics are sometimes accused of breaking the First Commandment by keeping statues, crucifixes and icons. The Church draws a sharp line here, and it does not fall where people expect: not between having an image and having none, but between what is done with it. An idol is a created thing treated as a god. A sacred image is a created thing that points beyond itself to God, or to those God has made holy.
strings.art.images.idol.title: An idol
strings.art.images.idol.body: Something made by human hands and then treated as divine — given the worship that belongs to God alone, or set in his place. The Catechism calls idolatry the divinising of what is not God, and it is not only carved gods: money, power, the state or one's own self can each be made an idol. This is what the First Commandment forbids.
strings.art.images.sacred.title: A sacred image
strings.art.images.sacred.body: A visible representation of Christ, his Mother, the angels or the saints. The material — wood, paint, plaster, bronze — is not holy in itself and no power resides in it. The image helps us remember and honour the one it shows, and the Church has always encouraged such images, above all because in the Incarnation the invisible God took visible flesh and so can be depicted.
strings.art.images.diff.title: The difference in a line
strings.art.images.diff.1: An idol is treated as a god; a sacred image represents Christ, Our Lady, an angel or a saint.
strings.art.images.diff.2: Worship is given to the idol itself; before a sacred image, worship is given to God and never to the object.
strings.art.images.diff.3: An idol takes God's place; a sacred image turns the mind towards him.
strings.art.images.diff.4: The First Commandment condemns the one and permits the other.
strings.art.images.bible.title: What Scripture shows
strings.art.images.bible.1: The same God who forbade idols commanded two golden cherubim to be carved for the Ark of the Covenant (Exodus 25:18–22).
strings.art.images.bible.2: He told Moses to make a bronze serpent and set it on a pole, and those who looked at it lived (Numbers 21:8–9).
strings.art.images.bible.3: Centuries later King Hezekiah destroyed that same serpent — because people had begun burning incense to it (2 Kings 18:4). The object had not changed; what people did with it had.
strings.art.images.honour.title: The honour passes to the one represented
strings.art.images.honour.body: When a Catholic kneels before a crucifix or kisses an icon, the reverence does not stop at the wood or the paint. It passes to the person shown, and in the end to God. Nobody prays to plaster. This is why veneration of an image is never the adoration owed to God alone — see Types of Reverence for the distinction between latria, hyperdulia and dulia.
strings.art.images.nicaea.title: The Church settled this in 787
strings.art.images.nicaea.body: The question was fought out in the iconoclast crisis, when images were smashed across the Byzantine world. The Second Council of Nicaea ruled that images of Christ and the saints may be kept and venerated, and gave the reason that has stood ever since: the honour shown to an image belongs to the person it represents, and adoration belongs to God alone.
strings.art.images.short.title: In short
strings.art.images.short.body: An idol says: this object is a god, and I worship it as a god. A sacred image says: this represents someone I honour, and my worship belongs to God alone. We do not worship statues. We worship God.
strings.art.images.quote: “The honour rendered to an image passes to its prototype.”
